source.title: Taming Polysemanticity in LLMs: Provable Feature Recovery via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Si-Yu Chen; Heejune Sheen; Xu-Yuan Xiong; Tianhao Wang; Zhuo-Ran Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and tests conditional SAE feature-recovery and identifiability claims, including a refinement that alternative factorizations may split features. It does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests feature identifiability and SAE feature recovery in a sparse-mixture model, plus consistency of learned SAE neurons across runs on Qwen2.5-1.5B. It does not test whether ordinary network neurons compete for capacity, whether real-model features are spread across native neurons, or the geometry of features emerging in the original toy models. Reconstruction-loss and activation-sparsity benchmarks, tuning ablations, and cited results from other work are not recorded as rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions. Several experimental results are described qualitatively while their plotted values are figure-only.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a method paper, and its main results are its own SAE's performance. It does, however, report results that bear on V5 (SAE features as stable, complete, canonical units). An identifiability theorem shows the minimal feature set is unique only up to permutation, rescaling and feature splitting. Planted-feature experiments show SAE recovery depends on co-occurrence, frequency and coefficient strength. Cross-seed consistency on Qwen2.5-1.5B shows TopK SAE features are seed-dependent and that consistency varies by method and neuron selection. None of these results measure native-neuron superposition, capacity competition or feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. It should add three points. First, GBA matches TopK on the reconstruction-sparsity frontier and is nearly tuning-free. Second, its features are more consistent across seeds than TopK's, but L1 is more consistent than GBA in 3 of 4 selection cases. Third, the authors frame identifiability as recovery of a minimal feature set up to permutation, scaling and feature splitting. They note the Gaussian-feature assumption and the difficulty of verifying incoherence in real data as limitations.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and analyzes bias adaptation and Group Bias Adaptation SAEs, rather than reproducing the original Toy Models of Superposition method. It uses a sparse nonnegative factorization model, theoretical dynamics analysis, synthetic feature-recovery experiments, and an SAE experiment on Qwen2.5-1.5B.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery changes with feature co-occurrence, target activation frequency and dimension, network width, feature occurrence, and coefficient cut-off strength. Real-data consistency comparisons depend on SAE method and on the neuron-selection criterion.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron selectivity: a feature of frequency f is learned by neurons whose target activation frequency lies roughly between f and √f. The authors liken this to resonance. It is supported by theory and by synthetic heatmaps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Which features an SAE recovers depends on the match between each latent's activation frequency and each feature's occurrence frequency.

record.problems: The dynamics guarantee relies on Gaussian-distributed features and simplifying assumptions. Synthetic tests use constructed ground-truth features; the Qwen experiment has no ground truth, so cross-run cosine consistency is only a proxy. The real-data consistency result covers one LLM, dataset, and layer. Many plotted empirical values are not reported numerically in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Reconstruction-loss and activation-sparsity method comparisons, GBA hyperparameter ablations, and neuron activation/Z-score analyses were omitted because they do not directly test the claim versions about feature identity, canonicality, or superposition geometry. Figure 6–7 scatter analyses were also omitted as supplementary consistency/property correlations; Figure 5 provides the direct cross-run consistency comparison.

untested.parts: No test of emergent superposition geometry, interference or a sparsity-dependent phase transition in trained toy networks. Incoherent features are assumed in the data model.
No test of capacity competition in native neurons, or of important features getting dedicated dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across native LLM neurons. There is no ground-truth recovery check in the LLM. Reconstruction-sparsity frontiers are method-performance results only.

Completeness of real-LLM SAE dictionaries, and whether real-model features satisfy the incoherence or decomposability assumptions. The authors say these are hard to verify. Consistency was tested only for Github data, layer 26.
Features are modelled as 1-D directions by assumption. Multi-dimensional features are never compared.

missing.what: Z-score vs cross-seed MCS scatter for GBA: higher-Z-score neurons are more consistent across seeds. For TopK (K=300), a smaller proportion of neurons exceeds MCS 0.9.
Histograms of maximum cosine similarity: a clear recovery peak appears only when ρ2 < 1/√n, and is absent at ρ2 = 1/√n.
GBA's activation percentage matches the true number of active features per sample (s=3) on planted data.

record.verdict_notes: The Qwen rows were relinked from V4 to V5 only: cross-seed consistency of SAE latents is a stability measure, not evidence of native superposition. Many synthetic results are figure-only, and the high-strength group rows (R7, R9, R11, R13) have no readable level. The study is not an original source for any version. Much of the paper reports its own method's performance (sparsity-loss frontier, ablations); these results are correctly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: The paper assumes near-incoherent feature directions and studies SAE recovery from sparse mixtures; it does not test emergent superposition geometry, interference, or a sparsity-dependent transition in toy networks.
No test of capacity competition in native neurons or of important features receiving dedicated dimensions while others share.
No test of whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.

Tests only indirect evidence from cross-run consistency of SAE neurons on one LLM setting; it does not measure native-feature spread across neurons or validate recovery against ground-truth LLM features.

Tests identifiability under the paper's statistical assumptions, synthetic recovery, and a consistency proxy on Qwen; it does not establish that learned real-model SAE dictionaries are complete or canonical.

The paper represents each ground-truth feature as a vector direction, but does not compare one-dimensional features against multi-dimensional features or test whether real-model features are one-dimensional.

rows.subject: decomposable dataset (statistical model)
rows.size_stated: X ∈ R^{N×d}; feature count n can be larger than d; N ≥ n is required in the discussion
rows.operation_detail: Proves ε-identifiability of the feature factorization under the stated decomposability assumptions.

conditions.value: nonnegative, row-wise s-sparse with s=Θ(1), non-degenerate coefficients, low co-occurrence ρ₂ ≪ n^{-1/2}

rows.measure: ε-identifiability of the feature matrix, allowing permutation, rescaling, and feature splitting
rows.note: The result identifies a minimal feature set up to the paper's equivalence, but permits an alternative factorization to refine or split each feature.
rows.check: The theorem gives uniqueness only of a minimal feature set. Alternative factorizations may split each feature, so canonicality holds only up to splitting. This is partial, not full, for V5. The result is also conditional on assumptions H1–H3 and V1.

rows.subject: Modified BA SAE (theoretical model)
rows.size_stated: M satisfies equation (6.5); n>d is allowed
rows.operation_detail: Analyzes Modified Bias Adaptation with fixed negative bias and spherical gradient descent.

conditions.value: X=HV satisfying Definition 5.2 and Theorem 6.1 conditions

rows.measure: alignment of a learned neuron with each true feature direction
rows.value: For every feature, a unique neuron reaches alignment at least 1−o(1) within T≤ς⁻¹ iterations.
rows.uncertainty: with probability at least 1−n⁻⁴ε over V
rows.note: This is a conditional theoretical guarantee for a simplified SAE training model, not evidence that all real-model SAE latents are canonical.

source_check.correct: For each feature, at least one neuron attains alignment ≥1−o(1) within T≤ς⁻¹ iterations, with probability ≥1−n^(−4ε) over V. Exactly one aligned neuron per feature is not guaranteed.
source_check.problem: The row overstates uniqueness: the guarantee is existence of at least one aligned neuron per feature.

rows.check: Cross-seed consistency of SAE latents bears on V5 stability, not on V4. It gives no evidence about native-neuron spread or ground-truth feature recovery in the LLM. Absolute percentages are figure-only. The comparison involves the authors' own method.

relationships.condition: Planted sparse-mixture data with Gaussian features, under the theorem's assumptions (n>d)
relationships.reason: The dynamics theorem guarantees a unique aligned neuron for every feature (R2). Empirically, GBA and TopK reach FRR close to 1 for n=4096, d=128 (R15, R16).
relationships.display_finding: The dynamics theorem guarantees a unique aligned neuron for every feature, and GBA and TopK reached feature recovery rates close to 1 at n=4096, d=128.
